pattern.name: Two pointers closing in on a sorted array
pattern.question: You add the smallest and the largest number and the sum is too big. Which of the two can never be part of the answer?
idea: In a sorted array the sum of the two ends tells you which end to move. If it is too big, the largest number is too large for every possible partner, so drop it. If it is too small, drop the smallest.
Each step throws away one number for good, so after at most n steps the pointers meet. No hash map is needed, which keeps the extra space at O(1).
spotWhen: The array is sorted and you look for a pair with a given sum or difference.
Extra memory must be O(1), so a hash map is not allowed.
Comparing the two ends tells you how to move.

dryRun.title: numbers = [1, 3, 4, 8, 11], target = 11
dryRun.note: The answer is given in 1-based positions, so indexes 1 and 3 are returned as [2, 4].

constraints: numbers is sorted in ascending order
Exactly one pair adds up to target
Positions are 1-based and the first position is smaller than the second
Target: O(n) time and O(1) extra space

approaches.name: Hash map of seen numbers
approaches.idea: Store each number and look for target - number. It ignores that the array is sorted.

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: Move the left or the right pointer depending on whether the sum is too small or too big.

why: Suppose the true answer is at positions a and b. As long as the pointers have not passed them, the sum of the current ends is bigger than target if the right pointer is past b, and smaller if the left pointer is before a. So the pointer that moves never skips the answer.
Every iteration moves one pointer by one step and they can move at most n steps in total. That is O(n) time with two integer variables.
mistakes: Returning 0-based positions. The problem asks for 1-based ones.
Using left <= right, which can pair a number with itself.
Moving both pointers on every step, which can skip the answer.
Sorting or building a hash map even though the array is already sorted.
variations: The array is not sorted. What is the best you can do?
Return all pairs that add up to the target (no repeats).
Find the pair whose sum is closest to the target.

pattern.name: Fix one number, then two pointers
pattern.question: If you already chose the first number of a triplet, what smaller problem is left, and which technique solves it fast?
idea: After you fix the first number a, you need two other numbers that add up to -a. That is exactly Two Sum on a sorted array, which two pointers solve in O(n).
Doing that for every first number gives O(n²). Sorting also puts equal values next to each other, so repeats can be skipped cheaply and every triplet appears once.
spotWhen: You look for a group of three (or more) values with a given sum.
The answer must contain unique combinations, no repeats.
Order inside the group does not matter, so you can sort first.

dryRun.title: nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] (sorted: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2])
rows: negative: left keeps moving right and the pointers meet with no triplet
same as the previous first number: skip
dryRun.note: The first number -1 appears twice. Index 2 is skipped, so the triplet [-1, 0, 1] is not reported a second time.

constraints: The array can have fewer than 3 numbers; then the answer is empty
The result has no duplicate triplets
Numbers can repeat and can be negative
Target: O(n²) time

approaches.name: Check every triplet
approaches.idea: Three loops, with a Set of sorted triplets to remove repeats.

approaches.name: Fix one number and use a hash set for the rest
approaches.idea: For each first number, solve Two Sum with a Set. Removing repeats is awkward.

approaches.name: Sort, then fix one and use two pointers
approaches.idea: Sorted order makes skipping repeats easy and needs no hash set. The space comes from the sorted copy.

why: After sorting, for a fixed first number the sum of the two pointers is monotonic: moving left right makes it bigger, moving right left makes it smaller. So the pair search is complete, like in Two Sum II.

Skipping equal first numbers and equal pointer values means each triplet value-combination is found once. The outer loop is n iterations and each pair search is O(n), so the time is O(n²). Sorting adds O(n log n) which is smaller.
mistakes: Not skipping equal first numbers, so the same triplet is returned many times.
After finding a triplet, moving only one pointer. That finds the same triplet again.
Forgetting the bound check left < right while skipping duplicates.
Sorting with the default sort(). It compares as text, so negative numbers and 10 versus 9 come out in the wrong order.
variations: Find the triplet whose sum is closest to a target.
Return the count of triplets with sum less than a target.

pattern.name: Move the limiting side
pattern.question: The water level is set by the shorter line. If you move the taller line inward, can the area ever get bigger?
idea: A container starts as wide as possible. Its water height is the shorter of the two lines. If you move the taller line inward, the width gets smaller and the shorter line is still the limit, so the area cannot grow.
Only moving the shorter line has a chance to find a taller limit. So at each step you move the shorter side and never lose a better container, which gives a single O(n) pass.
spotWhen: You choose two positions and the value depends on distance times a minimum.
Starting with the widest pair and shrinking is natural.
One of the two sides is clearly the one that limits the answer.

dryRun.title: height = [3, 9, 4, 8, 2]
rows: right is shorter: right = 1, pointers meet
dryRun.note: The best container uses lines 1 and 3: width 2 × height 8 = 16. Moving the shorter side each time still finds it.

constraints: height has at least 2 lines
Heights are non-negative integers
Lines cannot be tilted; the container is the area between two lines
Target: O(n) time

approaches.name: Try every pair of lines
approaches.idea: Two loops compute the area of each pair.

approaches.name: Two pointers, move the shorter line
approaches.idea: Start at the widest pair and always move the pointer at the shorter line.

why: Suppose the shorter line is on the left. Every container that uses this left line with a right line further inside is narrower and still limited by the same left line, so it is no better than the one we just measured. So the left line can be dropped safely.
Each step drops one line, so the loop runs at most n - 1 times: O(n) time and O(1) space.
mistakes: Using the taller line for the height instead of the shorter one.
Computing the width as right - left + 1. The width is the distance, right - left.
Moving the taller pointer, which can skip the best answer.
Returning the last area instead of the best one.
variations: Trapping Rain Water: how much water stays on top of the bars?
Return the indexes of the two lines, not the area.

pattern.name: Halve the exponent (fast power)
pattern.question: You know x^5. How can you get x^10 with one multiplication instead of five?
idea: A power can be built from a half power: x^10 = x^5 × x^5. So you only need to solve a problem half the size, then square the result. An odd exponent needs one extra × x.
Each call halves n, so a chain of about log₂(n) calls reaches the base case x^0 = 1. For a negative exponent, compute the positive power and take its reciprocal.
spotWhen: The answer for size n can be built from the answer for size n / 2.
A direct loop takes O(n) steps and n can be huge.
The half result can be reused, not recomputed.

dryRun.title: x = 2, n = 10
dryRun.note: The calls finish from the deepest one upward. For the odd exponent 5 the square of the half is multiplied by one more x.

constraints: n is an integer between -2³¹ and 2³¹ - 1
If n is negative, x is not 0
Do not use Math.pow or **
Target: O(log n) time

approaches.name: Multiply n times
approaches.idea: A loop multiplies x by itself n times. Far too slow for n near 2 billion.

approaches.name: Recursion that halves the exponent
approaches.idea: Compute x^(n/2) once, square it, and multiply by x if n is odd.

why: Mathematically x^n = (x^(n/2))² for even n and (x^(n/2))² × x for odd n, so a correct answer for n/2 gives a correct answer for n. The base case x^0 = 1 stops the recursion.
The exponent halves at each call, so there are about log₂(n) calls, each doing a constant amount of work. The call stack holds that many frames at once, which is O(log n) space.
mistakes: Writing myPow(x, n / 2) * myPow(x, n / 2). That calls the recursion twice and the time is O(n) again.
Using n / 2 for odd n without Math.floor, so n becomes a fraction and the recursion never reaches 0.
Forgetting the extra × x when n is odd.
Negating a very negative n after the recursion started, or computing 1 / x first when x can be 0.
variations: Write it with a loop and O(1) extra space (binary exponentiation).
Compute x^n modulo 1,000,000,007 for integer x.
Check whether a number is a power of two.

pattern.name: Swap the ends, shrink the range
pattern.question: After you swap the first and the last character, what is left to reverse?
idea: Swapping the first and last characters puts both in their final place. What remains is the same problem on the part between them, which is shorter by two characters.
That is a recursion in disguise: "reverse(range) = swap the ends, then reverse(inner range)". Writing it as a loop with two indexes gives the same result without using the call stack.
spotWhen: You must reverse or mirror a sequence in place.
The problem looks the same after the two ends are handled, just smaller.

dryRun.title: s = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
dryRun.note: Only n / 2 swaps are needed. The two pointers cross, so the middle never gets swapped with itself.

constraints: s is an array of single characters, and it can be empty
Reverse in place; return the same array
No second array
Target: O(n) time and O(1) extra space

approaches.name: Recursion on the inner range
approaches.idea: Swap the ends, then call the function for left + 1 and right - 1. The call stack grows with n.

approaches.name: Two-pointer loop
approaches.idea: Swap the ends in a loop and move both indexes inward.

why: After each swap the two outer positions hold their final values, and the unswapped part is the same problem on a shorter range. The loop ends when the range has one or zero characters, which are already in the right place.
There are about n / 2 swaps, so the time is O(n). Only two indexes are used, so the space is O(1). A recursive version needs a stack frame per swap and can overflow for 100,000 characters.
mistakes: Looping to s.length instead of the middle. Every pair is swapped twice and the array ends up unchanged.
Using left <= right. The middle element is swapped with itself, which is harmless, but with a recursion it can cause an extra call.
Building a new array with [...s].reverse() and not changing s.
Recursing without a base case, or on a very long array, which overflows the call stack.
variations: Reverse the words of a sentence, but not the letters inside each word.
Reverse only the vowels of a string.
Check whether a string is a palindrome using the same two pointers.
